title: The wooden huts of Antarctica

paragraphs.text: Sitting on my desk is an illegal acquisition, a black pebble the size of a walnut, I picked it up some years ago when I visited Ross Island in Antarctica.This vast wilderness of rock and ice on the Ross Sea is one of the most breathtaking spots on Earth, looking south over a tremendous ice shelf and north to sweeping ocean icebergs. But it is forbidden to take anything from this land. No matter that removing my pebble had as much impact as taking a grain of sand from the Sahara. Those who decide the fate of Antarctica have declared it their own and only they can remove bits of it.

I found the stone near a rather nondescript wooden cabin on the shores of Ross Island. This is one of two small huts which were built during one of the classic episodes of exploration, the legendary contest between Britons Robert Scott and Ernest Shackleton, and Norwegian Roald Amundsen, to be the first man to reach the south pole. Amundsen was the eventual winner in this epic battle of endurance. The huts, Shackleton's at Cape Royds (built in 1908) and Scott's at Cape Evans (constructed in 1911) are still full of the supplies left behind by each expedition. Both Scott and Shackleton endured intense privation on the way to their respective failures, yet their exploits became synonymous with bravery. In the case of all three explorers, science had been an excuse for what was, in truth, a bid for personal and national glory. Shackleton's long retreat in 1917 ended the heroic age of polar exploration. The Antarctic was then left in relative peace by the outside world for half a century.

But the huts survive, in place and intact, as surely, they should be. They are protected in part by their remote location. Inside, their contents are literally frozen in time. There are bunks and sleeping bags, skis and snowshoes, hanging legs of ham, sacks of powdered milk and row upon row of jars and tins of food and other supplies. No other continent I know of retains the physical traces of man's first attempts at settlement and his subsequent and inevitable eviction by Mother Nature. This is not just history as artefact, but artefact as story, and story as vivid reality. Such mementos are rare and precious.

The huts are occasionally visited by scientists and also by a few ship-borne tourists who can get ashore in summer. They are, however, in deep trouble. They are being slowly looted by visitors keen to take mementos of their trip back home, and time and weather are destabilising them. Jet pollution from a military airbase hangs over them and nearby lies a new highway, built by the military, to the south pole. The question of how to save the huts from further destruction is controversial and tough. Should they be kept as they are now, certainly recognisable, but partly looted and disarranged? Should their contents be replaced by facsimiles or conserved as found, rusted and tattered? Or should they be restored to the state they were in when they were left, with the men exhausted, their hopes dashed and hell outside?

The state of the huts also raises the more basic dilemma of whether or not tourists should be allowed in these most virgin wastes of ice. Tourism in Antarctica has quadrupled in the past decade or so and continues to accelerate, despite the sinking in November 2007 of a cruise ship that hit an iceberg. Numbers rose in 2007 by 14% to 37,000, almost all by sea. Despite growing interest, tourists are banned from staying ashore overnight by the 1959 international Antarctic treaty and there are a vast array of regulations as to what they can and cannot do.

Tourists are distrusted by scientists, who were granted the right to use the continent for their research by the Antarctic treaty, which proclaimed the region to belong to all the peoples of the world. The 1959 treaty is often held up as a rare example of effective international negotiation, even though Antarctica is protected by geographical vastness and ferocious weather conditions. But the scientists are reluctant to relinquish that right or share it with others. Annual Antarctic conferences yield such headlines as 'Tourism threat to the Earth's last great wilderness.' Scientists apparently pose no threat. This double standard is well illustrated in the Lonely Planet guidebook to Antarctica, with its stunning photographs. This includes a furious warning that tourists should not pick up rocks or even feathers to take back as mementos. But this prohibition is printed alongside a scientist boasting of the riches he has gathered from the place: 'The problem is not in finding the fossils but in deciding which ones to collect. '

I cannot see why nobody except scientists, certain military outfits and eccentric explorers should be permitted to visit Antarctica. The condemnation of tourists for daring to encroach on this landscape is unacceptable. It is not a destination for the masses. Antarctica is too distant and costly, and tolerable only in summer. But anyone, suitably monitored, should be allowed to enjoy the wonders of the polar regions, as of the world's deserts and forests. Ice is ecologically fragile, but these lands are enormous.

Besides, the best ambassadors for polar conservation are those who pay good money to see Antarctica and then go home and write glowing reports. What is certain is that people will continue to arrive in Antarctica in ever larger numbers, and they will want to see relics of the heroic frozen past. All the more reason that those two small wooden huts deserve to be carefully protected and preserved.

groups.title: Who has the right to visit Antarctica?
content: The Antarctic treaty is usually seen as a success story for global {{35}} . However, it could be regarded as unnecessary because the region is protected not only by its {{36}} but by the extreme nature of its climate. Despite Antarctica belonging to all the people of the world, there are double standards regarding access to the area. While scientists are not seen as a potential {{37}} , tourists are. For example, scientists may remove any number of fossils from Antarctica, but tourists are forbidden to take any {{38}} . It is not likely that Antarctica will become a mass tourist destination. Therefore, visitors who have appropriate supervision should be given full access. In fact, allowing tourists to visit the region simply encourages them to become {{39}} of protection for the region.
